philosophy.meta.title: Philosophy
philosophy.meta.description: A letter from the person building One Day Investor: invest one day a month, ignore the other thirty.
philosophy.hero.label: Philosophy
philosophy.hero.subtitle: A letter from the person building One Day Investor.
philosophy.ritual.label: The ritual
philosophy.ritual.title: Why a month, not a day.
philosophy.ritual.p1: I don't want to check the markets every day. I don't think you should either.
philosophy.ritual.p2: Most financial apps are built on an assumption I don't share: that more frequent data is more useful data. So they give you notifications, intraday charts, red and green arrows, a little dopamine hit every time your portfolio moves. The implicit message is: pay attention, you might miss something.
philosophy.ritual.p3: One Day Investor is built on the opposite assumption. You almost certainly won't miss anything. The things that actually matter to your long-term wealth — jobs, savings rate, whether you kept investing through the scary months — move at the speed of months and years, not minutes.
philosophy.ritual.p4b: one day a month, you open the app and write down where your money is.
philosophy.ritual.p4c: That's it. The other thirty days, you live your life.
philosophy.ritual.p5: I don't track a specific goal with a specific number and a specific date. I don't know how much I'll need in twenty years. I don't know what I'll spend it on. What I do know is that I want the line to go up over time — not every month, but on average, over enough months that a trend is visible. That's the whole game.
philosophy.ritual.quote: The market is fast. Wealth is slow. Don't confuse them.
philosophy.gaps.label: Positioning
philosophy.gaps.title: Two gaps no bank can fill.
philosophy.gaps.intro: Your bank is better than One Day Investor at almost everything. It knows your exact balance to the kopeck, it processes your transactions, it sends you statements. I'm not trying to replace any of that. There are two specific things, though, that no bank can do for you — and they happen to be the only two things I actually care about.
philosophy.gaps.bank.label: What a bank shows you
philosophy.gaps.bank.1: One account, or at best one family of accounts.
philosophy.gaps.bank.3: History that resets when you switch banks.
philosophy.gaps.bank.4: Nothing about the apartment, the car, the cash under the mattress.
philosophy.gaps.odi.label: What One Day Investor shows you
philosophy.gaps.odi.1: Every pocket you own, in one place.
philosophy.gaps.odi.2: One net worth number, in your chosen currency.
philosophy.gaps.odi.3: A line that outlives any bank you ever use.
philosophy.gaps.odi.4: Everything that has a price — including the things banks can't see.
philosophy.gaps.closing: The banks will keep being banks. I just want to give you the two things they can't.
philosophy.deal.label: The deal
philosophy.deal.title: What I do for you. What you do yourself.
philosophy.deal.p1: I want to be honest about where the work lives, because most "all-in-one finance apps" are a little dishonest about this. The ones that promise total automation either connect to your bank (fragile, scary, and not how I want to build software) or quietly skip everything that doesn't have an API (which is most of what you actually own).
philosophy.deal.auto.label: Automatic
philosophy.deal.auto.1: Exchange rates to your base currency
philosophy.deal.auto.4: Total capital, always recalculated for you
philosophy.deal.manual.label: By hand, once a month
philosophy.deal.manual.2: Share and crypto quantities (if they changed)
philosophy.deal.closing: No bank integrations. No open banking. I physically can't touch your money, and I never will. That's not a compromise, that's the design. You already know where your money is — you just need a place to write it down that doesn't feel like a spreadsheet.
philosophy.pockets.label: Organization
philosophy.pockets.title: Pockets, the way you already think.
philosophy.pockets.p1a: When I ask someone where their money is, they don't say "40% equities, 30% fixed income, 20% cash, 10% alternatives." They say:
philosophy.pockets.p1b: "Some at Tinkoff, some at Interactive Brokers, the apartment, a bit of crypto, and whatever's in my wallet."
philosophy.pockets.p2: That's how pockets work in One Day Investor. A pocket is wherever you mentally keep a chunk of your net worth. One per account, or one per thing, or one per category — whatever matches the map that already lives in your head.
philosophy.pockets.p3: If you actually invest in Lego sets, Lego is a pocket. If your apartment is half of your net worth, the apartment is a pocket. Nothing is a second-class citizen here, because the real point isn't taxonomy — it's making sure nothing gets left out when you do the monthly write-down.
philosophy.audience.label: Audience
philosophy.audience.title: Who this is for.
philosophy.audience.quote: If you already invest — calmly, imperfectly, without a spreadsheet — this is for you.
philosophy.audience.p1: You probably already have a brokerage account. Maybe some crypto. Maybe an apartment, maybe a savings account in a different currency, maybe a little cash. You think of your money as something you're trying to grow, not something you're trying to optimize.
philosophy.audience.p2: You are not a day trader. You don't want to be one. You don't need Sharpe ratios, you don't care about rebalancing algorithms, and you've never wanted a "portfolio analytics dashboard."
philosophy.audience.p3: You just want to know — honestly, monthly, in one number — whether the line is going up.
philosophy.audience.p4: If that's you, I built this for us.
philosophy.closing.author: — Vlad, building One Day Investor
